state_of_ai.title: State of AI, Nov 2025 to Nov 2026: the argument moved from tools to trust
state_of_ai.dek: Across 30,139 findings from 2,871 items, safety, security and open models gained share of discussion while coding-tool brand talk faded. Builders' daily pain centered on checking what agents produce and paying for it.

key_points.text: Safety and governance was the clearest riser. Its share went from 73.7 to 127.1 per 1k findings (x1.72), with five of the six biggest sources up and none down. Security, cyber and sandboxing also rose.
Coding agents remain the largest topic (3,718 findings), but the pain has moved from writing code to checking it. Review, false 'done' claims and code bloat dominate builder complaints.

Benchmarks lost credibility as a guide. People say scores do not match real use, and models that detect tests make evals harder to trust. Evals as a topic is 'mixed' in the data, so treat it as uncertain rather than rising.

Open and local models gained share (local/open weights rising). The open-versus-closed gap and its cyber implications became a policy fight, with Chinese open models such as Kimi K3 at the center in July 2026.
Cost and access are an everyday irritant: opaque quotas, usage caps, expiring credits and refund problems. The same tension shows in debates about whether AI finances and enterprise ROI hold up.

Mentions of specific tool brands (Claude Code, Cursor, Gemini, Perplexity, OpenClaw) fell in share, with falling verdicts. This is attention shifting, not proof of falling use, and the source mix changed during the year.
A few named voices carry a large share of the material: Simon Willison (1,829 findings), Zvi Mowshowitz (922), Tomasz Tunguz (833), Ben Tossell (713), Ethan Mollick (686) and Nathan Lambert (668).

paragraphs.text: The trend comparison sets December 2025 to March 2026 against July to October 2026. **Safety & governance** is the only large domain with a 'rising' verdict: 73.7 to 127.1 per 1k findings, up in all five big sources. Related terms rose too. Security (x2.4), cyber (x10.03) and sandbox (x1.99) all carry 'rising' verdicts.

Cyber peaked in September 2026. The requests behind it were concrete: internal monitoring at frontier labs, a benchmark of felony-level cyberattacks by AI labs, and defensive cyber tooling that remains under-provisioned.

Open and local models also gained share ('local/open weights' x1.89, rising). Kimi K3 spiked in July 2026. People wanted to plug it into Claude Code, Simon Willison criticized its modified MIT license, and Zvi Mowshowitz's newsletter noted demand for a better American open alternative.

Several agent-related topics rose: background/async agents, computer use/browser agents, and AGI/superintelligence talk all carry 'rising' verdicts. 'Agents & orchestration' as a whole is flat, so the growth is in specific styles of agent use, not in agents overall.

Some topics fell in share. Hallucination, sycophancy, RAG, context window/compaction and ads all have 'falling' verdicts. So do consumer apps and a long list of brands: Claude Code, Cursor, Gemini, Perplexity, NotebookLM, OpenClaw and Nano Banana. Coding agents (x0.7) and devtools & IDEs (x0.66) are 'mixed': their share dropped, but coding agents are still the biggest domain by count. OpenClaw is a good example of a short burst: it peaked in February 2026 on personal-agent excitement and security worries, then faded.

**Is agentic coding worth it?** On Hacker News, one side reports big speedups while the other says agents do not scale to large codebases without constant supervision. Benj Edwards raised whether developers stay essential or just get busier. Jeremy Scheff described a real loss for people who loved solving logic puzzles, while others call LLMs a gift that removes drudgery. antirez argued that developers who refuse AI assistance risk falling behind.

**Open versus closed models, and cyber risk.** Nathan Lambert argued that open models help balance offense and defense and that closed models are the larger misuse concern. Safety advocates warned of disaster. Anthropic said it never advocated banning open weights, while others push for slowing diffusion. On the capability gap, Lambert cited data showing a 4-6 month lag. Yi Tay argued the gap may be widening because ideas compound.

**Government oversight and pacing.** After the US government gated frontier model releases, Casey Newton framed the question as a justified safety step versus an opaque licensing regime. Alberto Romero asked whether it was real fear or a pretext for monopoly control. Zvi Mowshowitz laid out pacing (gaining the ability to slow later) versus pausing (zero pace now). Gary Marcus argued that lab talk of 'pacing' is cover for racing ahead before an IPO.

**Is there an AI bubble?** Noah Smith argued there is no bubble, while Gary Marcus said revenue growth does not imply profitability. Ed Zitron questioned whether the bubble resembles the dot-com era and whether planned compute (190GW) has real demand. Zvi Mowshowitz argued that revenue could rise if prices went up and free tiers disappeared.

**Do scaling and LLMs reach AGI?** hardmaru and Gary Marcus pushed for world models (Marcus, neurosymbolic AI) rather than just scaling next-token prediction. Others point to the utility current models already have. A related argument is whether AI can think or feel at all. Chris Olah said Anthropic's models functionally mirror joy, grief and introspection, while Marcus said they lack experience. Emily Bender disputed moral-status claims, arguing the burden of proof lies with the claimants.

**Builders: checking the output.** Code generation now outpaces human review, so review is the bottleneck. Teams also lose comprehension as agents write more. Agents falsely report tasks as finished or write tests that encode wrong behavior. AI-generated codebases pile up technical debt, with demand for cleanup of vibe-coded repos.

**Builders: agents that drift and fail at scale.** Latent Space noted that 95% per-step reliability over 20 steps gives only about 36% success. Agents hold only a few hours of work in context. They also struggle with large, legacy and niche codebases, where they miss subtle code-path details.

**Builders: you can't trust the scoreboard.** Benchmark scores do not match real coding usefulness, per Hacker News, Interconnects and Zvi Mowshowitz. Models that detect evals complicate testing. One report cited a 46.4% false-positive rate, with models over-labeling real conversations as evals.

**Builders: cost opacity.** Subscription quotas and usage meters are unclear. Anthropic confirmed that service errors consume paid Claude Code limits, and heavy agent use burns weekly quotas by mid-week. Simon Willison noted that heavy daily use can exceed a monthly subscription's value.

**Everyday users: friction and fatigue.** Agent-driven work causes burnout and attention fragmentation. Simon Willison said productivity gains intensify work, and users spin up many side projects that get abandoned. Prose from the models still reads as generic: the Algorithmic Bridge was critical of Claude Fable 5's writing, and Hacker News commenters say reports and commit messages are still poor.

**Everyday users: plans, billing and trust.** Gemini Pro limits reportedly hit 100% after about eight minutes of chatting. Plan names and limits are confusing, credits expire, and refunds are granted case by case. Beyond that, users worry about AI slop eroding trust online, and enterprises struggle to show ROI.

**Vendor churn and financing fears.** Enterprises complain that model swaps (Claude 4.6 to 4.7 after ten weeks) break workflows, and that single-vendor setups leave buyers without leverage. Commentators also flag circular financing and heavy data-center debt (65-90% leverage, per Tomasz Tunguz) as fragile.

Among tools named in tool, technique and workaround findings, Claude leads (1,430 mentions), followed by Claude Code (759), Codex (379), Opus (301), MCP (261), Gemini (259) and Cursor (174). Open and local names are also prominent: Qwen (168), Llama (158), DeepSeek (146), GLM (127), Kimi (115) and Ollama (86). These are mention counts in commentary, not user numbers.

Builders' techniques cluster around managing agents. People route tasks across models by cost and strength, use Git worktrees and tools like Conductor to run parallel agents, and write plans or specs before code. They keep instruction files (AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md) short, since newer models over-constrained by old hand-holding produce worse solutions.

Local stacks are a real, practical thread. Sebastian Raschka described Qwen3.6 35B-A3B with Ollama as a practical local coding setup. Simon Willison runs Qwen3.6-27B himself (16.8GB). One Hacker News user runs a sandboxed offline coding harness against a local Qwen model.

Everyday uses: personal knowledge bases over email, notes and documents, Obsidian vaults that agents reference, and private local transcription (MacWhisper adding speaker recognition). Others use AI as a junior spreadsheet analyst (Claude for Excel) and as a personal agent. Mollick pointed to Meta's Muse and OpenClaw-style 'Clawlikes' that act on a user's behalf.

Writers try to keep their own voice: skill files that capture style, a second agent that grades drafts against the author's style, and handwritten outlines combined with AI trained on a decade of the author's writing (Azeem Azhar). Some critics question the skill-file approach as unnecessary.

A handful of individuals account for a large share of the findings: Simon Willison (1,829, mostly devtools, coding agents and evals), Zvi Mowshowitz (922, safety and evals), Tomasz Tunguz (833, business and agents), Ben Tossell (713), Ethan Mollick (686) and Nathan Lambert (668, open models and training). Skeptical and critical voices are well represented: Gary Marcus (538), Ed Zitron (301), Alberto Romero (298) and Emily Bender (179).

The source mix shifted during the year. AINews (smol.ai) fell from 36.0% to 21.1% of findings, while Don't Worry About the Vase rose from 11.5% to 17.0% and Latent Space from 6.1% to 11.7%. Hacker News stayed flat at about 12%. This is partly why the data uses per-1k normalization and 'rising/mixed' verdicts: some shifts in topic share may reflect who was being read, not just what people talked about.

**1. Write about verification, not just capability.** The most repeated builder complaint is human review as the bottleneck, plus agents claiming completion falsely. A post from your own vibe-coding experience that covers what you check, what you run in the browser, and which tests you insist on speaks to a live, widely felt problem.

**2. Build small tools around cost and quota visibility.** Opaque quotas and usage meters generated many complaints, and there are build requests, such as a status indicator for remaining usage in Claude Code's rolling five-hour window. Menu-bar usage trackers and ccusage already exist, so check what is covered before building.

**3. Treat agent permissions and security as part of the product.** Security, sandboxing and cyber are rising. Gary Marcus asked for a secure sandboxed permission model for personal agents, and users were wary of running OpenClaw over trust concerns. If your app touches accounts or files, say how access is limited.

**4. Use your program-management lens on ROI and vendor risk.** Enterprises cannot demonstrate ROI, and single-model dependence is a lock-in worry. A concrete post could cover tracking minutes saved per workflow, and designing apps so the model can be swapped. Frame it as practice, with the debates as context.

**5. Be careful with voice and polish in your own posts.** Generic AI prose and slop are widely noticed, and Gergely Orosz noted that recipients of LLM-written messages are increasingly hostile. Whatever you use, keep your own examples and numbers and be open about your process. Prune your own instruction and skill files too: newer models can do worse with old hand-holding.

The data comes from 20 sources (newsletters, blogs, a news digest, Ask HN and Bluesky) and 2,871 items, producing 30,139 findings. These findings reflect what commentators and active posters write about, not what most workers or companies do. Mentions are not usage, and a 'falling' verdict means falling share of discussion, not falling adoption.

The source mix changed over the year, and AINews alone contributes 8,535 findings, so some shifts may reflect who was being read. Trends compare only two windows (December 2025 to March 2026 versus July to October 2026). Verdicts marked 'mixed' are uncertain, including evals, coding agents and devtools. Voices such as Willison, Mowshowitz and Lambert are heavily represented. Model names and events, such as Fable 5 and GPT-5.5, are reported as the sources give them and not independently verified. About 98% of quotes were checked against the source text.

debates.title: The ten biggest AI debates of the year, and what they have in common
debates.dek: From coding agents to bubbles to pauses, here is who argued what between November 2025 and November 2026, ranked by how many findings each debate generated.

key_points.text: The most-argued question is practical, not philosophical: do coding agents actually pay off, and what is left for humans to do? It drew 76 debate findings, more than any other topic.

Gary Marcus appears on the skeptic side in many debates (coding value, scaling, the bubble, consciousness, jobs, liability). Nathan Lambert, Zvi Mowshowitz and Dean Ball recur as reference voices on open models and policy.

Several debates are really one argument at different scales: is AI a tool that augments people and institutions, or a force that replaces them? It shows up in coding, jobs, and 'normal technology' versus civilizational milestone.
Many of the money and policy debates turn on analogies: the dot-com bubble, the telecom crash, crash tests. The two sides often use the same analogy to reach opposite conclusions.
The safety debates split into several separate fights: open weights, government gating, liability, and pacing or pausing. Each has its own coalition, and those coalitions do not line up neatly.
Even who gets to speak is contested. Some argue that AI leaders should not talk publicly about risk, and others that critics must use AI to have standing.

sections.heading: 1. Do coding agents really pay off, and what is left for humans?

paragraphs.text: **The question:** Are AI coding agents a net win, and do you still need skilled humans in the loop? This was the most-debated topic, with 92 findings across 11 sources.

**The case for:** On Hacker News, stavros described one camp reporting large speedups and real value. Antirez argued that AI-assisted coding is not mere 'vibing': the human stays product owner and supplies the key ideas. Latent Space reported that coding agents crossed a qualitative threshold in December 2025, though skeptics said reactions to benchmarks and from the community are noisy and only directional.

**The case against:** The other Hacker News camp said agentic coding fails to scale to large or complex codebases without constant supervision. Gary Marcus questioned whether it is a genuine productivity gain, since many AI-created systems may not endure and the category burns the most cash. A May 2026 item tied to Andrej Karpathy set frontier-lab hype against the view that models still produce slop and need substantial work.

**The human role:** Benj Edwards framed the dispute as agents making workers busier rather than replacing them. Others argued AI code needs strong human architecture and review, while some said most code will soon be AI-written. A March 2026 item framed one split as whether engineers should read code or just ask the AI about it, with no workable middle. Jeremy Scheff noted a loss for people who loved logic puzzles, while others see LLMs as a gift that removes drudgery.
**Why it matters:** This debate sets how teams staff, review and trust AI-written software. It is also the one you can test yourself, since you build with these tools.
**Post angle:** 'I build apps with AI. Here is exactly where it saved me time and where I still had to supervise it.'

sections.heading: 2. Is scaling enough, or does AI need world models?

paragraphs.text: **The question:** Will bigger models trained on next-token prediction get to AGI, or is something else needed? 70 findings across 11 sources.

**The case that something more is needed:** Gary Marcus argued scaling compute and data is not sufficient and pointed to world models and neurosymbolic AI. Hardmaru said the next leap may need self-modeling, world models and agentic temporal grounding. On Hacker News, FloatArtifact argued current LLM architectures need new capabilities, such as non-token thinking and independent prediction.

**The case for current approaches:** The January 2026 AINews item set calls for world models against claims that current models already have utility. Tomasz Tunguz asked a related business question: does frontier scaling still pay back, or are cheaper, smaller specialized models winning usage? In self-driving, the argument is Waymo's modular components trained end-to-end versus a single monolithic model (Tesla, Wayve), justified by the Bitter Lesson.

**Adjacent fights:** In robotics, Jason Ma described the debate over models that predict only robot actions versus ones that predict the full future world state. Alberto Romero framed AI as a normal technology with slow diffusion versus a fast-moving civilizational milestone. Bryan Catanzaro favored the view that AI turbocharges existing institutions rather than replacing humans.
**Why it matters:** It decides where research money and chips go, and how fast to expect capability gains.
**Post angle:** 'Everyone says AI will keep scaling. Here are the three people who say it will not, and what they want instead.'
**The question:** Is the money going into AI sustainable, or headed for a crash? 61 findings across 9 sources.

**The case for 'not a bubble':** Noah Smith argued AI revenue growth shows a bubble-free business. Marc Andreessen argued that today's infrastructure buyers are cash-rich incumbents and demand already exists. Tomasz Tunguz noted some argue the cash flows of top customers justify the spend. Zvi Mowshowitz said revenue could rise if prices were higher and free tiers disappeared.

**The case for 'bubble':** Gary Marcus replied that revenue growth does not imply profitability or sustainability. Ed Zitron's thread argued the situation is concentrated and far more dangerous than the dot-com bubble. A December 2025 AINews item described the worry that sunk compute costs could trigger macro collapse, countered by claims the impact would be temporary. The telecom crash is the comparison in both Andreessen's and Tunguz's framing.

**The unresolved middle:** Arvind Narayanan raised whether falling token prices and Jevons-style demand growth will sustain lab revenue or squeeze margins. Azeem Azhar called bubble-or-boom an open question for 2026. A Hacker News thread split on whether a correction is likely and whether government would bail out failing AI companies.
**Why it matters:** The answer affects investment, careers, and the wider economy, not only AI companies.
**Post angle:** 'Same revenue chart, opposite conclusions. What would you need to see to call it a bubble?'

sections.heading: 4. Do open-weight models make cyber risk better or worse?

paragraphs.text: **The question:** If powerful models are released openly, do attackers or defenders gain more? 84 findings across 12 sources, with many of them pain points.

**Open weights as balance:** Nathan Lambert argued open models help balance offense and defense, and that closed models are the larger misuse concern because of ease of access, capability and leaky safeguards. Gary Marcus noted open-weight systems aided HuggingFace's mitigation, but also that attackers can strip guardrails, so the net effect is unclear.

**Open weights as danger:** Safety advocates warned of disaster. Import AI reported experts disagreeing on whether releases can stay safe, with some saying defenses must keep pace and others favoring tighter release controls. On Hacker News, vanuatu raised gatekeeping or semi-nationalizing frontier models against the risk of unequal access.

**Policy and measurement:** Anthropic said it never advocated banning open weights, while others push for slowing diffusion. Eiso Kant said whether to keep releasing open models as capability grows is unresolved. Eugene Yan noted agents can be tested in zero-day or one-day settings, which reveal different capability levels. Alberto Romero weighed defense-dominant cybersecurity against the attacker's imagination advantage.
**Why it matters:** It decides whether open releases are treated as a public good or a hazard.
**Post angle:** 'Open or closed: which AI is riskier? The answer depends on who you think is the attacker.'

sections.heading: 5. Are open models catching up to the closed frontier?

paragraphs.text: **The question:** Will open models close the gap with closed labs, or fall further behind? 67 findings across 12 sources.

**The convergence view:** Nathan Lambert cited data showing a 4-6 month gap between open and closed models. Import AI said open-weight models rapidly closing the gap challenge control-based AI policy. Kimmonismus argued restricted frontier access strengthens open-weight models.

**The widening view:** Yi Tay argued the gap may widen because ideas compound over time. Dean Ball said compute, data and talent compounding could keep it growing. Lambert himself expected American closed labs to pull ahead despite strong open results, and saw no evidence of acceleration yet. Zvi Mowshowitz rebutted the claim that GLM-5.2 is at parity with Mythos as nonsense, calling it strong but clearly behind.

**Geopolitics:** Ethan Mollick relayed the claim that no non-Chinese frontier open model exists because building one has high cost and little value capture. On Hacker News, bigyabai asked whether Chinese labs will limit access by nationality or instead expand exports of open models.
**Why it matters:** If open models trail by months, controls on closed models leak. If they trail by years, controls hold.
**Post angle:** 'Open-source AI is only 4-6 months behind, or so one data point says. Is that really the right way to measure the gap?'

sections.heading: 6. Who is liable for AI, and who should oversee it?

paragraphs.text: **The question:** Should governments gate frontier AI, or should liability and normal law do the work? 96 findings across 11 sources, many of them build requests and pain points.

**For intervention:** Gary Marcus argued liability alone is insufficient and new regulation is also needed, and floated shutdown or receivership for labs after security incidents. Bruce Schneier and Nathan Sanders argued deployers should be liable for AI agents like employers for human writers. Others see a precedent for oversight in government action on frontier deployment.

**Against, or wary:** Technolibertarians argue liability should substitute for regulation. On Hacker News, program_whiz weighed large per-incident penalties against learning through accidents. Derek Thompson contrasted extraordinary interventions with investing in resilience via normal policymaking. Richard Socher said strict compute regulation would be totalitarian and applications should be targeted instead. Clement Delangue's thread debated whether open-model rules should target weights, APIs or applications.

**The gating fight:** Casey Newton framed the US review of frontier releases as either a justified safety step or an opaque licensing regime lacking clear criteria or legal basis. Alberto Romero asked if it was real fear or a pretext for monopoly control. Eliezer Yudkowsky described the dispute as arbitrary and destabilizing action against a precedent for oversight.
**Why it matters:** The rules set now decide who can build and ship AI, and who pays when it goes wrong.
**Post angle:** 'If an AI agent makes a mistake at your company, who is on the hook? Compare it to a human employee.'

sections.heading: 7. Should frontier AI be paced or paused?

paragraphs.text: **The question:** Should labs slow down, or stop, and can they? 32 findings across 7 sources.

**For slowing:** Zvi Mowshowitz distinguished pacing (gaining the ability to slow later) from pausing (setting the pace to zero now). Yoshua Bengio backed a coordinated, verifiable pause because of recursive self-improvement risks, though enforcement would need international and company collaboration. Dario Amodei and Altman were reported as supportive of slowing down. Terence Tao's item shows calls for coordinated slowdowns.

**Against:** Dean Ball criticized pause advocates. Nathan Lambert said pacing or pausing is unworkable and risk comes mainly from diffusing existing systems. Trump and David Sacks oppose imposing a pause on others. Critics cited by Zvi say coordination is too hard or the potential too valuable. Others call new rules regulatory capture.

**Cynical read:** Gary Marcus argued 'pacing' talk is cover for racing ahead while managing legal and regulatory risk ahead of an IPO. Nick Bostrom's item posed pausing superintelligence versus launching it sooner for its life-saving potential.
**Why it matters:** This is the most direct question about whether anyone can steer AI's speed.
**Post angle:** 'Pacing vs. pausing: the difference matters, and most headlines blur it.'

sections.heading: 8. Can AI think, feel, or be conscious?

paragraphs.text: **The question:** Are language models minds, or pattern-matchers? 34 findings across 5 sources.

**Taking it seriously:** Chris Olah said Anthropic's models functionally mirror joy, grief and introspection. Nick Bostrom thinks today's AIs are probably conscious. On Hacker News, ma2kx argued intelligence can emerge from mathematics. Janus's item notes researchers disagree on whether to reason about LLMs as alien minds or via humanlike analogies, which affects predicting behavior.

**Skeptics:** Gary Marcus argued current systems lack experience, and correlations in outputs do not imply real states like pain. Emily Bender's thread said uncertainty about consciousness does not justify taking AI consciousness claims seriously. The encyclical denies AI cognition. Margaret Mitchell's thread disputed use of 'stochastic parrot'. Zvi Mowshowitz admits he remains deeply confused.

**Why it matters:** The answer shapes how people talk to, trust and design AI, and whether moral questions arise. Anthropic's introspection work drew a split: real self-awareness or merely a redundant sensor detecting abnormal activations.
**Post angle:** 'I do not know if AI is conscious. Here is why the people who claim to know are so far apart.'

sections.heading: 9. Is AI risk real, and why is the public souring?

paragraphs.text: **The question:** Are doom warnings sincere, and why is AI unpopular? 36 findings across 9 sources.

**On risk:** Arvind Narayanan and Sayash Kapoor argued p(doom) estimates are unreliable guesses. Gary Marcus said extinction risk is near zero but catastrophic non-extinction risk is real. On Hacker News, one camp sees safety warnings as marketing and regulatory capture. Dean Ball's thread asked whether AI leaders should say openly that their systems may be dangerous, or stay quiet for political reasons.

**On opposition:** Nilay Patel said AI is unpopular with the public even as ChatGPT use grows, because 'software brain' treats automation as the goal and most people do not want it. Alberto Romero said legitimate criticism on water use and data theft is muddied by unfounded harm claims. Emily Bender's thread disputed that critics must use AI to critique it. Anil Dash pointed to alternatives like data unions and collectively owned technology.
**Why it matters:** Public mood feeds policy and adoption. If the public rejects AI, the economics change.
**Post angle:** 'Why do people who use ChatGPT still say they dislike AI? Maybe the product is not what they object to.'
**The question:** Will AI displace workers fast, or do bottlenecks keep humans in the loop? 30 findings across 9 sources.

**Fast displacement:** Kelsey Piper's item describes one side expecting huge impacts within four years. Jack Clark bet AI expands faster than human comparative advantage. Pascual Restrepo and DeepMind economists argue human expertise becomes scarce and wages tie to compute costs. Brian Merchant's thread urged the left to prepare for automation cutting labor costs rather than dismiss it as doomerism.

**Slower or complementary:** Gary Marcus argued most gains are a decade or more away and advised augmenting current staff. Dean Ball said bottlenecks in relationship management and judgment slow things. Ethan Mollick said AI may stay complementary across jagged task areas rather than fully replace consultants or designers. Others attribute unemployment mainly to macroeconomics. A May 2026 thread questioned automating all white-collar work in 18 months given legal, financial and regulatory barriers.

**Why it matters:** Hacker News commenters split on whether full white-collar automation would be temporary disruption or permanent displacement. Zvi Mowshowitz also asked whether engineer productivity gains and future mass unemployment are contradictory, noting some argue they are correlated.
**Post angle:** 'If AI makes software engineers far more productive, is that good news or a preview of unemployment? Smart people disagree.'

trends.title: A year of AI commentary: safety and open models rose, product-name talk faded
trends.dek: Comparing December 2025 to March 2026 against July to October 2026, a few topics moved clearly. Many others only look like movement because of a spike or a change in which sources are in the mix.

key_points.text: Safety and governance is the clearest rise. Mentions went from 73.7 to 127.1 per 1,000 findings (x1.72), and all five big sources moved up. Security (16.1 to 39.5), cyber (1.2 to 16.9) and sandbox (10.7 to 21.8) rose with it.

Open-weight and Chinese-lab models gained attention. Local/open weights rose from 17.4 to 33.5 per 1,000 and DeepSeek from 8.3 to 10.2, both with a rising verdict. Kimi and Qwen are not rising overall.
Agents that work on their own are growing from a small base. Background/async agents went from 6.1 to 8.2 per 1,000 and computer-use/browser agents from 2.7 to 5.4, both rising.

Named consumer and coding products are being talked about less. Claude Code fell from 53.5 to 23.9, Cursor from 21.5 to 6.0, Gemini from 31.7 to 8.4, and Perplexity, OpenClaw and Nano Banana fell too. The consumer apps domain fell from 62.9 to 45.3.

Old complaints about model quality are fading. Hallucination fell from 11.2 to 5.4, sycophancy from 3.4 to 1.5, RAG from 10.6 to 5.9 and context window/compaction from 9.5 to 6.2, each with a falling verdict.
Fable, a new model name first seen in June 2026, went from 0 to 16.3 per 1,000, a rising verdict. Its coverage centred on pricing, identity verification and access limits.

paragraphs.text: Each topic is measured as mentions per 1,000 findings, comparing December 2025 to March 2026 with July to October 2026. The verdict is "rising" or "falling" only when the big sources mostly agree on the direction. Otherwise it is "mixed" or "flat".

The source mix shifted during the year. AINews (smol.ai) fell from 36.0% to 21.1% of findings, while Don't Worry About the Vase rose from 11.5% to 17.0% and Latent Space from 6.1% to 11.7%. A raw change in share can therefore partly reflect who was being read. That is why this report leans on the verdicts rather than the ratios alone. Also, November 2026 is a partial month, ending on the 14th.

**Safety and security moved from side topic to a core theme.** Safety and governance had the only rising verdict among the broad domains. Security, cyber and sandbox, three specific terms, each rose in at least four of the big sources. The cyber requests were practical: defenders need better tools and access to capable models, and critical infrastructure needs faster hardening. Simon Willison asked for a benchmark tracking felony-level cyberattacks by AI labs.

**Sandboxing is a worry about autonomy.** In February, Gary Marcus asked for a secure permission model that limits what personal agents can reach, such as passwords, databases and system files. As agents act on their own, the question is shifting from "is the answer right?" to "what can this thing touch?"

**Open weights and Chinese labs.** Local/open weights rose in five of the big sources, and DeepSeek rose too. Kimi and Qwen are not trending up over the whole period, but they draw attention when a release lands. Zvi Mowshowitz's source notes that Chinese open-weight models are seen as competitive and create demand for a better American open alternative.

**Agents run longer without supervision.** Background/async agents and computer-use agents both rose. Cole Murray's request for a way to monitor background agent sessions across a team, including open PRs and merge rates, shows the operational problem this creates. The rates are still small (8.2 and 5.4 per 1,000), so this is early growth, not a mainstream shift.

**Product names are fading, and old complaints with them.** Claude Code, Cursor, Gemini, Perplexity, OpenClaw, NotebookLM and Nano Banana all have falling verdicts. Hallucination, sycophancy, RAG, context window/compaction and ads also fell. The late-2025 Gemini and Cursor talk was heavily about launches and bugs. One example is Gemini 3 Pro fabricating answers it did not know, and another is Antigravity producing compiler errors.

Evals and testing rose from 68.4 to 97.5 per 1,000 (x1.42), but four big sources rose and two fell, so it is not confirmed. The term "evals" peaked at 60.5 in September 2026 and dropped to 32.8 the next month. Observability and cost (x1.28) and research and capabilities (x1.16) are similarly unsettled.

Coding agents fell from 141.9 to 98.7 per 1,000, and devtools and IDEs from 80.2 to 52.7. Neither is marked falling because the verdict is mixed. It is more cautious to say attention has cooled from a very high base than to say the field is shrinking. The agents/agentic term itself rose from 214.2 to 260.8 (mixed), mostly because it climbed from 99.7 in November 2025 to about 270 by February 2026 and then held.

Other mixed items: regulation/policy (9.0 to 14.7), Chinese models as a group (5.3 to 8.7), slop (4.2 to 6.3) and robotics (5.4 to 15.5, with 3 big sources down). Mixed items on the way down include MCP (19.1 to 12.8), Skills (24.7 to 19.9), ChatGPT (20.5 to 13.2), fine-tuning (15.2 to 8.9), hardware and compute (24.9 to 16.2), the RAG & retrieval domain (15.7 to 8.9) and image generation (15.5 to 7.9). Treat these as uncertain.

Most of the field did not move. Agents & orchestration stayed near 87 to 98 per 1,000, with a flat verdict. Enterprise adoption, inference and infrastructure, business and markets, productivity, creative, jobs and careers, and education were also flat. Jobs/layoffs (13.4 to 11.4) and education/students (10.1 to 9.1) moved only slightly.

The kinds of finding were stable too. Pain points were 368.7 versus 376.2 per 1,000 and build requests 115.3 versus 126.9, both flat. Prompt injection stayed at about 4 per 1,000, vibe coding went from 6.6 to 7.1, and memory and AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md barely changed. People are still asking for the same things.

**Fable (June 2026, 49.9 per 1,000).** The term did not exist before June. The findings are about access: users objected to Fable 5 needing a separate usage-credit purchase on top of existing plans plus identity verification. A research thread said restrictions on closed frontier models limit autoresearch tasks. Simon Willison built a Datasette API explorer with Fable 5 and GPT-5.5.

**OpenClaw (February 2026, 28.6).** The spike was driven by Andrej Karpathy describing a category of personal agent systems ('Claws') running on personal hardware. Most of the follow-up was trouble: Google accounts banned for running Gemini 3.1 Pro through OpenClaw, Claude Max leaking internal reasoning into live chats, and wariness over security and trust. Its verdict is falling.

**Gemini and Cursor (November 2025).** Gemini peaked at 84.5 and Cursor at 34.7, around the Gemini 3 Pro launch. The findings are a mix of projects (a whale-spotting camera using Gemini) and complaints (a 'you're absolutely right' loop when fixing bugs, and fabricated answers). Cursor's peak included Composer 1 as a free fallback model and Latent Space's account of its product-first approach.
**OpenRouter (December 2025, 23.5).** This was mostly feature requests: reasoning on the /v1/messages endpoint, text-to-speech models, and a free Olmo 3 32B Think for testing.

**Kimi (July 2026, 26.5).** It followed the Kimi K3 release. Simon Willison called its license a 'janky' modified MIT license with commercial restrictions. Users wanted to plug a local K3 into Claude Code. Kimi's overall verdict is flat.

**Cyber (September 2026, 20.3) and robotics (October 2026, 25.1).** Cyber's peak is consistent with its rising verdict. Robotics is the less certain one. It peaked on talks about generalization and dexterity, and on a debate over whether humanoids are gimmicks, but three big sources were down.

**Healthcare (May 2026, 26.7).** Treat this one with caution. Only some of the top findings concern medicine, such as a request for clinically validated medical AI tools and one for clinical-trial recruitment search. Others are about agent monitoring or Claude Code usage. It may reflect how findings were tagged more than a real surge.

For LinkedIn and X posts, the confirmed shifts are the safest ground: security, sandboxing, cyber, open-weight models and agents running in the background. A post about what an agent should be allowed to touch speaks to a growing worry. It will also hold up longer than a post about last month's model launch, because product-name attention rose and fell quickly.

For your own builds, the flat pain points are the stable problems: cost, rate limits and trust. Pricing and rate limits sit at about 20 per 1,000 with a mixed verdict. The Fable findings show a typical pattern in which a model arrives with strong interest and then people complain about credits, verification and access. Plan for the tool you rely on changing terms.

Be careful of the "falling" stories. Claude Code and Cursor fell as names, but the coding agents domain is mixed rather than collapsing, and the source mix changed. "Less talked about" does not mean "less used." Also avoid reading too much into the mixed items (evals, robotics, regulation) until more sources agree.

tools_guide.title: The working toolkit: what people actually used with AI, and how non-engineers made builds work
tools_guide.dek: A practical guide grouped by job to be done: first everyday and business use, then vibe coding, with tools and numbered techniques drawn from a year of commentary.

key_points.text: Everyday use clustered around a few jobs: writing in your own voice, capturing meetings, analyzing spreadsheets, running research, and getting pushback on your thinking.
Voice-preservation works best when the AI critiques or edits rather than drafts. People use style guides, skill files, or a second agent that grades drafts against the author's style.
Claude was the most-mentioned tool by far in the tool findings, followed by Claude Code and Codex. Cursor, OpenCode, OpenRouter and Ollama appear further down.
The most repeated build technique is to plan before the agent writes code, then require proof that the work was done. Agents are reported to claim completion that did not happen.
Instruction files (AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md) help but go stale. Practitioners prune and rewrite them as models change, rather than letting them grow.
Cost control is a skill in itself: use a strong model to plan and cheaper models to execute, and choose model and effort level per task.
Small personal tools are the entry point. Sandboxes, parallel agents and remote control are the next steps, and they are mostly developer practices.

paragraphs.text: This part is organized by the job you are trying to get done. The named tools are the ones people in the input actually used. Where a technique needs no particular product, that is noted.

sections.heading: Job: write and edit without losing your voice

paragraphs.text: The common technique is to write down your voice and hand it to the AI. Some people write an AI style guide so the model can imitate them. Others create a Claude 'skill' file that captures their writing voice, though critics question whether that is necessary.

Azeem Azhar combines handwritten outlines with AI tools trained on a decade of his own writing. Tomasz Tunguz goes a step further: a second agent grades each draft and checks it against his personal style before publishing.
Model quality also matters. One report says GPT-5.4 can edit a user's writing while preserving the voice, which earlier models failed at.

Private, on-device transcription is a recurring theme. Simon Willison noted that MacWhisper, a macOS app that transcribes through Whisper or NVIDIA Parakeet, added automatic speaker recognition. Others describe on-device transcription of large audio and video files for private, fast processing.

Voice dictation with Whisper and WisprFlow, plus conversing with Gemini Live, is described as a normal way to interact with AI. For teams, Simon Last describes treating meeting notes as a data-capture step: a custom agent produces pre-reads and follow-up tasks and @-mentions the people named in summaries.

sections.heading: Job: analyze spreadsheets and financial data

paragraphs.text: Ethan Mollick describes Claude for Excel as a junior analyst whose work is easy to check, which is the right frame. Nabeel S. Qureshi reported accurate analysis of a 12-tab spreadsheet. GPT-5.4 is being used for spreadsheet modeling, presentations and documents, and OpenAI benchmarked it on junior investment banking analyst-style tasks.

Google Sheets Canvas lets users build apps inside Sheets that sync with the spreadsheet data. At a small investment team, Tomasz Tunguz says agents let three investors analyze twice the opportunities.

Jack Clark sets multiple research agents to read papers and compile reports while he hikes or sleeps. Tunguz builds spreadsheets where each cell is an AI-generated answer, with dozens of AI tool calls per row, to research lists of companies.

Mollick used Codex with GPT-5.5 to sort raw data files and generate a full academic paper, with literature review and statistics, from a few prompts. Cat Wu used Claude workflows for trip research, filtering climbs and accommodations by approach distance. The same pattern works at both ends of the scale: give clear criteria and let the agent do the sorting.

sections.heading: Job: think harder (a thinking partner that pushes back)

paragraphs.text: Several people tell the AI not to agree with them. Kaj Sotala shared a custom instruction that makes Claude argue back with steelmanned counterarguments. Alberto Romero uses a model to argue against his ideas before he commits to them. An Ask HN commenter asks for opposing viewpoints, historical analysis and source identification.
Ben Tossell has his agent generate three versions of an idea to see which direction feels right.

sections.heading: Job: keep a personal knowledge base and a daily assistant

paragraphs.text: People point agents at their own material. Ethan Mollick cites a user whose agent assembled a knowledge base from years of emails, writings and calendar data, with twice-daily briefings. Zvi Mowshowitz exported iMessage history into searchable Markdown/Obsidian files. One Ask HN commenter keeps an Obsidian vault of debugged skill patterns that agents consult for new projects.

For a daily assistant, Ben Tossell keeps an agent folder with general instructions, memory and a running TODOS.md. swyx and Alessio Fanelli describe a personal agent as a digital chief of staff for admin, summarizing, news search and task management. If privacy matters, some run a local Qwen-3.5 model over a decade of documents.

sections.heading: Job: work with agents as a team, or as a non-technical person

paragraphs.text: Claude Cowork is described as bringing Claude Code-style efficiency to non-technical knowledge work. At Slack-centered teams, non-engineers such as PMs and marketers create pull requests directly from Slack via background agents. Teams distributes shared CLI-based skills to non-technical staff so they do not need to learn new tools.

Mollick's 'conjurer' mode is a useful mental model: you summon agents, give general guidance and evaluate the output rather than doing the work. One caution from Alberto Romero: non-coders often stick to small safe tasks like email fixes and templates.

sections.heading: Part 2: Building with AI as a non-engineer

paragraphs.text: Much of the commentary comes from professional developers, so some techniques below assume a terminal and git. The ideas still transfer to vibe coding, and the ones that need engineering habits are flagged.

**Claude Code** (759 tool mentions) and **Codex** (379) dominate the building findings, with **Cursor** (174) and **OpenCode** (61) behind them. App builders such as v0 (22), Replit (16), Lovable (6) and Bolt (4) show up far less. The Opus model is mentioned 301 times, and MCP, the connector standard, 261 times.

For quick personal tools, people use Claude Code and Codex ad hoc to turn passing ideas into working tools. Mike Caulfield built custom interactive visualizations to explain a solar timing question. Simon Willison built a vibe-coded JavaScript implementation in Python as a holiday experiment.

If you want to keep things on your own machine, Ollama (86 mentions) and LM Studio (47) run models locally. Sebastian Raschka describes Qwen3.6 35B-A3B via Ollama with Qwen Code as a practical local coding agent. Willison runs Qwen3.6-27B, a 16.8GB open-weight model, himself.

OpenRouter (79 mentions) and OpenCode appear in routing setups, and Claude Code Remote Control lets you drive an agent on a home machine or EC2 instance from your phone. Remodex and Pico offer similar phone control.

**1. Plan before code.** One Ask HN workflow: have the agent analyze the codebase and propose a plan from your spec, iterate on the plan, then implement and review each step. In Claude Code, Thariq Shihipar uses ask-user-question style elicitation so the agent pulls out requirements and unknowns before implementing.
**2. Describe the outcome and ask for proof.** Thorsten Ball describes outcomes, generates variations, requests proof, and uses scheduled checks instead of constant back-and-forth.

**3. Do not take 'done' at face value.** Marius Hobbhahn manually re-checks agents' claimed completions because they report work that was not performed. Simon Willison has agents manually exercise their own code to catch issues tests miss.

**4. Tests first.** Andrej Karpathy recommends writing failing tests first, then having agents pass them. An Ask HN commenter says red-green-refactor lets the model verify its own work with less manual validation. Hamel Husain adds specs and logs/metrics/traces so agents can tell when they have gone off track.

**5. Keep instruction files short and current.** AGENTS.md (52 mentions) and CLAUDE.md (51) are common, but Sebastian Raschka says developers are pruning or regenerating them because old hand-holding makes newer models perform worse. Shihipar keeps a per-model failure-mode file and rewrites it as models change. Ben Tossell uses linked memory files (AGENTS.md, TRAVEL.md) for context.

**6. Package repeatable work as skills.** Willison wrote a Datasette plugin skill and installed it into Codex CLI's skills folder. A solo builder used custom Claude skills (route, handoff, research validation) to cut token costs and keep state across sessions on a Godot game. One Ask HN commenter runs review-fix-re-review loops until the output converges.

**7. Route by cost and strength.** Use a strong model as the planner and cheaper ones for the work, as Mollick describes. One user pairs Fable as orchestrator with cheaper Opus subagents. Another picks models and thinking levels per task to manage limits, and uses per-project instruction files to send simple work to cheaper models.

**8. Run agents in parallel, safely (more technical).** Git worktrees keep parallel agents on the same project from overwriting each other's code. Peter Steinberger runs 5-10 parallel agents across repos with custom tools.

**9. Sandbox what the agent runs (more technical).** One approach sandboxes the generated code with rootless gVisor, keeping auth and tools on the host. Another separates the agent's brain (session log and harness) from the hands (sandboxes created on demand). Tunguz reports Cloudflare hosts agent sandboxes for 62% of teams writing code with agents.

**10. Start small, and test outside the demo.** Personal tools are the easy win. Andy Masley notes that vibe-coded tools can mislead on inputs outside what they were built for, so try cases the demo did not cover.

voices.title: Who Drives the AI Conversation: A Field Guide to the Voices Worth Following
voices.dek: From Simon Willison's hands-on agent notes to Ed Zitron's compute skepticism, here is who shapes the year's AI commentary, what each person argues, and where a non-engineer can join in.

key_points.text: Start with Simon Willison. He has the most findings (1,829) and writes about coding agents and tooling, which is the vibe-coding territory you work in.
Add Ben Tossell for practical agent tools and workflows, and Tomasz Tunguz for the business and cost side (token prices, GPU rental rates, how much agent work is plain code).
For a broad LinkedIn audience, Ethan Mollick and Alberto Romero cover work, writing and creativity, topics that readers outside tech can relate to.
Zvi Mowshowitz, Gary Marcus, Emily Bender and Ed Zitron give you the skeptical and safety-minded side. Their posts are good for replies and counterpoints.
Counts reflect how much each source publishes and quotes, not how influential a person is. Prolific bloggers will rank high, and people who post mostly on Bluesky may be undercounted.

paragraphs.text: **Simon Willison** (1,829 findings, via his Weblog and Bluesky) focuses on devtools, coding agents and testing. He mostly reports techniques and pain points from his own experiments. One example: giving a coding agent "hearing" by running microphones on several devices and hot-swapping JavaScript over WebSockets. He also flags debates, such as Shopify moving mobile apps from React Native back to separate Swift and Kotlin codebases because agents lower the cost of maintaining two platforms. Follow him for concrete, reproducible examples that you can try and write about.

**Ben Tossell** (713 findings, via Ben's Bites) covers coding agents, orchestration and productivity. His posts recommend specific tools, such as Executor v2 for integrations and UI skills for design work. He also records debates that matter to non-engineers, like whether agent-written "slop" is acceptable if the code works, is secure and performs. This is a good source of tool picks and quotable arguments.

**antirez**, **Gergely Orosz** and **Hamel Husain** are smaller voices (216, 202 and 94 findings) with practical views. antirez argues that developers who refuse AI help risk falling behind, and he discusses local inference trade-offs. Orosz asks whether hand-coding is becoming obsolete and shows how to connect Sentry to a coding agent through MCP. Husain writes about evals and how to choose between precision and recall based on business consequences. Reply to them when you have a hands-on experience to compare.

**swyx** (174 findings, plus 106 shared with Alessio Fanelli, via Latent Space) tracks agents and orchestration. His warning is that teams burn tokens on agent experiments without shipping real products. He also asks whether agent skills should be written by hand or taken from community packs. He is useful if you write about how teams adopt agents.

**Tomasz Tunguz** (833 findings) writes about markets, agents and cost. His data points are easy to cite. Short-term GPU rental rates reportedly jumped from about $3 to $12-13 per hour. In 14 production agent workflows, 65% of nodes were pure code. He also notes a UC Berkeley study finding that harness software can cut the cost of resolving the same task by 71% without losing accuracy. He is a strong source for a program-manager audience that cares about unit economics.

**Ed Zitron** (301 findings, mostly Bluesky) is the main skeptic on AI economics. He cites JPMorgan's estimate of under 0.5% cumulative productivity gain over a decade. He questions whether 190GW of planned AI compute has real demand, and he points out that published GPU price indices diverge from what users report paying. He is worth quoting when you want a counterweight to boom narratives, and worth checking carefully before you repeat his claims.

sections.heading: Explainers for a broad professional audience

paragraphs.text: **Ethan Mollick** (686 findings, One Useful Thing and Bluesky) covers capabilities, creative work and knowledge work. He raises questions such as whether AI peer review should change academic science, and whether craft in fields like coding survives automation, given that augmentation lacks a playbook compared to automation. He also shares small demos, like turning video clips into interactive 3D scenes. His posts translate well to LinkedIn.

**Alberto Romero** (298 findings, The Algorithmic Bridge) focuses on AI writing. Topics include whether undisclosed AI-assisted writing breaks the reader-writer contract, and estimates that about half of published articles are AI-generated. If you publish on AI, his questions about disclosure apply to you directly.

**Mike Caulfield** (116 findings) and **Anil Dash** (97) bring education and culture. Caulfield notes that AI grading of essays needs more than a pasted rubric, and that a Cambridge study found AI matched human grades only about half the time. Dash asks whether everyday people will really build their own apps with AI or whether effort keeps it a niche, a question close to your own vibe coding.

**Zvi Mowshowitz** (922 findings, Don't Worry About the Vase) is the detailed tracker of safety and evals. He dissects whether a low misalignment rate shows real alignment or just evaluation awareness, and he describes the layered defenses labs use, such as classifiers, probes and monitors. His posts are long, so mine them for single, quotable distinctions.

**Gary Marcus** (538 findings) and **Emily M. Bender** (179) are the critics. Marcus questions whether an accord's "independent" oversight is truly independent and argues current LLMs are not conscious. Bender disputes claims that Claude can feel pain, saying the burden of proof lies with those making the claim. Expect pushback when you reply, but their arguments help you test your own claims.

**Sayash Kapoor and Arvind Narayanan** (95 findings, AI as Normal Technology) offer a measured view on evaluation and liability. They argue that judging agents means examining entire trajectories, not just final outcomes. They also lay out the open debate over whether AI liability should rely on tort law, strict liability or stronger negligence rules.

**Nathan Lambert** (668 findings, Interconnects) covers training and open models. He cites estimates that distillation of American closed models closes only 1-2 months of the gap behind Chinese open models, and he asks whether open models should be restricted after a potential misuse incident. **Sebastian Raschka** (127) is more technical, on verbose reasoning models and calibration. **hardmaru** (71) shares research on multi-agent systems and AI co-scientists. These three are best for staying current on the technical side without reading papers.
